newsitem.title: FRANCE: Security tight in Paris as Islamists' trial opens.
newsitem.headline: Security tight in Paris as Islamists' trial opens.

text.p: Thirty-four Moslem fundamentalists accused of backing Moroccan guerrillas went on trial in Paris on Monday under tight security as police said they feared new attacks after a train bombing in which four people died.

Investigators say plans to try the militants may have motivated the bombers, who struck six days ago, blasting a rush-hour train at the Port Royal station near the French capital's sprawling Luxembourg Gardens.
The cases have not been formally linked but anonymous telephone threats have been received warning of fresh attacks unless France releases detained Moslem fundamentalists.
Only 21 of the 34 accused were in the dock as the trial began.

Six others, including three French passport-holders, were in detention in Morocco -- three of them awaiting execution and three sentenced to life terms there. Another, Algerian Djamel Lounici, was detained in Italy. The rest are being sought by the authorities.

The 34 are accused of criminal conspiracy in connection with a terrorist enterprise. They are alleged to have backed guerrilla violence in Morocco in 1994, including the robbery of a Marrakesh hotel in which two Spanish tourists were shot dead and a gunfight with police in Fez.

They were among nearly 200 Moslem fundamentalists detained after a wave of bomb attacks in France in 1995 in which eight people were killed and 160 injured. Algeria's Armed Islamic Group (GIA) claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying France supported the military-backed Algerian government.

Nearly all of the accused are French Moslems in their mid and late 20s, children of Algerian or Moroccan immigrants recruited in run-down, high-rise suburbs near Paris, Orleans and the eastern town of Besancon which have large Arab minorities.
Prosecutors say they were recruited by Morocco's outlawed Islamic Youth Movement whose aim was to overthrow King Hassan and create an Islamic government.
The group also had support from Algerian fundamentalists. Lounici is accused of membership of the armed wing of the Algerian Islamic Salvation front (FIS).
The prosecution says the accused were sent for weapons training aboard, including Afghanistan, and that they carried out hold-ups in France as well as Morocco to finance their activities.
But most of their missions were either botched or not carried out at all, according to the prosecutors.
Officials said 20 people were still in hospital after last Tuesday's train bombing. Another 92 had been treated for wounds or shock.
Investigators say they suspect the bomb was set off by Algerian Moslem rebels because of similarities to the 1995 wave of attacks.
France has sent its European neighbours a list of 13 possible suspects in the latest Paris bombing, all of them believed to be Islamic activists.
